title: The pull request workflow
objective: By the end of this lesson you can take a change from branch to merged through a pull request, and you understand what the workflow is protecting that direct pushes do not.

blocks.text: A pull request is not a Git feature — it is a convention built on top of Git by hosting platforms. It says: here is a branch, here is what it changes, please look before this becomes part of the shared work. Everything it adds is social and procedural, and that is exactly the point.

blocks.caption: One change, start to finish
lines: git switch main && git pull                     # start from today's state
git switch -c fix/upload-limit                  # a branch named for its purpose
git add -p                                      # stage deliberately, hunk by hunk
# open the pull request on the platform
# respond to review comments with more commits
# merge when approved and checks pass
git switch main && git pull                     # bring the merged work back down

blocks.title: git add -p is worth the extra minute
blocks.text: It walks you through each change and asks whether to stage it. You catch the debug line, the accidental formatting change, and the unrelated edit — before they become part of a commit someone else has to read.
What a reviewer needs from you

items: A title that states the effect, not the activity — 'Reject uploads over 10MB', not 'fix upload'
A description that says why this change exists and what you decided against
A branch that does one thing; a pull request touching four unrelated areas gets a shallow review
Commits that make sense in order, tidied with interactive rebase before you ask for eyes
Anything the reviewer cannot see: how you tested it, what you could not test, what you are unsure about

blocks.title: Size is the strongest predictor of review quality
blocks.text: A 50-line change gets read line by line. A 2,000-line change gets skimmed and approved, because thorough review of it would take hours nobody has. If a change must be large, say so and point reviewers at the parts that matter — or split it into a sequence of pull requests that each stand alone.

blocks.caption: Push more commits; do not rewrite mid-review
lines: git commit -m "Move the size check into the validator"
git push                       # the pull request updates automatically
# Once review has started, avoid amending or force-pushing:
# it invalidates the comments reviewers already left.

rows: Keeps every commit and records the join
Branches whose individual commits are meaningful
Collapses the branch into one commit on the shared branch
Most feature branches; keeps the shared history clean
Replays the commits with no merge commit
Teams that require a strictly linear history

blocks.text: Squash is the common default because it makes one shared-history entry per change, which is usually the right granularity for anyone reading main later. The individual commits still exist in the pull request record if anyone needs them.
Protection rules: why the branch refuses direct pushes

items: Require a pull request, so nothing lands without a second pair of eyes
Require approvals, and require them again when new commits arrive
Require status checks to pass — tests, linting, build
Forbid force pushes to the shared branch, which is what stops history from being rewritten under everyone
Restrict who may merge, for branches that go to production

blocks.title: The protection you will resent, once
blocks.text: The day you need to fix something urgently, the rules will be in your way. That is what they are for: the same barrier that slows an emergency fix also stops an unreviewed change at 2am from reaching production. Teams that add an emergency bypass usually find it becomes the normal path within a month.

blocks.title: Rehearse the loop locally
steps: In ~/git-lab: git switch main && git pull
Edit a file, then run: git add -p        (choose y/n per change)
Run: git commit -m "Reject values over the limit"
Run: git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD   (exactly what a reviewer would see)
Run: git switch main && git merge fix/demo-limit && git push
Run: git branch -d fix/demo-limit && git push origin --delete fix/demo-limit
blocks.expected: The full cycle without a hosting platform: branch, staged deliberately, pushed, the exact review scope listed, merged, and both copies of the branch cleaned up. On a real platform only the review step is added.

cheatsheet: A pull request is a platform convention on top of Git, not a Git feature
Start from an updated shared branch; branch names state their purpose
git add -p stages change by change and catches what you did not mean to include
Title states the effect; description says why and what you rejected
One concern per pull request — size is the strongest predictor of review quality
Respond to review with new commits; do not amend or force-push mid-review
Squash and merge is the usual default: one clean entry per change on the shared branch
Protection rules require review and passing checks and forbid force pushes
After merging: pull the shared branch, delete the branch locally and on the server

checkpoint.prompt: What is a pull request, technically?

choices.A: A convention provided by hosting platforms
choices.B: A Git command that requests a merge

checkpoint.explanation: A request to review a branch before it joins the shared work. Git itself has no such concept. The platform adds review, discussion, and gating around an ordinary branch.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does the size of a change matter so much for review?

choices.C: Small changes get read line by line

checkpoint.explanation: Large ones get skimmed and approved because a thorough review would take hours. Review quality falls off sharply with size. Splitting a change into independently reviewable pieces gets you real review rather than a rubber stamp.

checkpoint.prompt: A reviewer has left comments. How should you make the requested changes?

choices.A: Add new commits and push them
choices.B: Amend the original commit and force-push
choices.C: Close the pull request and open a new one

checkpoint.explanation: Existing comments stay anchored to what they referred to. Rewriting during review detaches the comments from the code they were about, and reviewers lose their place. Tidy the history before review starts, not during.

checkpoint.prompt: What does forbidding force pushes on a shared branch protect against?

choices.B: History being rewritten under everyone who has it
choices.D: Slow clones because the branch history is too long

checkpoint.explanation: It is the rule that keeps the shared history append-only, which is what makes everyone's copy trustworthy. Rewriting means silently removing commits from the shared branch.
